### Multicollision correction

Choosing a fork to inspect no longer retires the chain; every fork remains flippable.
The table prints choices in stage order, matching the displayed blocks. New searches
retire the previous chain immediately. Independent verification now binds each fork
to its predecessor and each message to its stated mask, and checks complete-set counts.
Mutation replay reads structured test results and rejects crashes or setup failures.

Cancellation in degraded mode is checked before computation starts and on every
progress update or error, so a retired run cannot replace a newer result.

## Deviations from the brief

- **HH-2: retain the hardened mutation runner.** Restoring the base text-search runner would allow a timeout, crash or setup error to masquerade as a kill. The current structured-report validation remains. The repair also clears generated output and captures the baseline bundle hash immediately after an explicit clean build; browser artifact collection had left stale mutant chunks beside the active bundle. A kill still requires the named assertion to fail, a changed successful build, restoration to the original build hash and a passing restored test.
- **HH-12: salted hits are measured, not forced to zero.** A twelve-bit table can accidentally return a valid salted preimage. The visible “TABLE USELESS FOR THIS BATCH” appears only when every table candidate fails verification; the recovery experiment reports the actual count. Under an ideal independent random-function model, a domain of N=4096 with M=2624 stored unsalted outputs has per-user accidental-success probability M(2N−1)/N³. The resulting probability of at least one hit among 20 users is about 0.624%, rather than the audit summary's 0.3%. The extra contribution comes from the table candidate sometimes being the originally sampled password. This is a model calculation, not a guaranteed or measured frequency.
- **Existing accessibility oracles were not weakened.** The audit's condensed files retained the contrast/non-text algorithms. The full reference structure and comments are restored, and missing structural boot assertions now check list semantics, one main landmark, seven tabs, the skip-link destination, default inputs, closed disclosures and absence of theme controls. The lab-specific state driver remains adapted to Hash Hunt.

## Audit repair evidence

HH-1 now has both a genuine same-type eight-bit collision control and a deterministic Floyd run with four actual same-type retries before the cross-type forgery. The page logs the rejected letter pairs, and browser tests hash those letters with Node SHA-256. Separate mutations bypass the semantic verifier and the retry step.

The salt-timing test exercises the real inline fallback and observes the actual CSPRNG calls. Each salt must be drawn after the real table-build completion callback. A mutation creates the targets before construction, and must fail that test; this is distinct from the existing invalid-bucket-answer mutation. Table construction still has no access to salts. The experiment uses the full lookup table as described on the page.

The full lookup is named Bcrypt Forge’s Scenario B; Hash Zoo, DNSSEC Chain, Feistel Forge and Grover have framed links. Non-byte-aligned controls expose the final-byte mask and measured cap. Explicit Hellman/rainbow start-point fixtures confirm that an index is not accepted as a preimage merely because it is a stored start.

Counts are obtained with `npx vitest list --json`, `npm test` (which expands parameter rows to 37), `npx playwright test --list` (23 claims plus two accessibility drives), and the 24-entry `scripts/mutations.json`. No tests are skipped. Local browser runs can select an installed Chromium with `CHROMIUM_PATH`; the registered port, deployment workflow, header and theme pin are unchanged.

Mutation restoration hashes the JavaScript files listed by each fresh Vite build manifest. Unreferenced files left by browser artifact collection are excluded; baseline, mutant and restored builds still have to satisfy every assertion and hash check.

readme_sections.heading: What Can Go Wrong
readme_sections.text:
- A valid tag over a collision-prone digest does not establish which letter was approved.
- Two active Floyd registers exclude seeds, hash state, counters and diagnostics.
- Full lookup covers reachable digests, not all outputs. H(x) targets differ from uniform output targets.
- Hellman's roughly 0.63 model requires the stated parameter relation and heuristic independence. Rainbow's recurrence is a random-function model, not a measured success rate.
- Matching endpoints still require regeneration and verification. Diagnostic coverage/merge sets consume extra temporary memory.
- Salts prevent mapping reuse, not per-user guessing. At 12 bits, accidental valid table answers and multiple preimages are possible.
- Joux multicollisions are not second-preimage attacks. Kelsey–Schneier long-message second-preimage techniques remain out of scope, and no result on this page breaks real SHA-256.
- A public, unkeyed mapping lets an adversary search for colliding table buckets offline. Here the measured cost is the number of table slots inspected during insertion, not SHA-256 collision work. The keyed HMAC comparison is a toy countermeasure illustration, not a benchmark or proof that every server resists denial of service. The selected names, table size and probing algorithm are identical between runs; only the bucket mapping changes. See [Rust's current `HashMap` documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.HashMap.html) and [Aumasson and Bernstein's SipHash paper (2012)](https://www.aumasson.jp/siphash/siphash.pdf).
- Runtime caps may stop a search. Input changes retire old results; cancellation terminates the worker. Bounded fallback can occupy the main thread if workers cannot be created.

readme:
# Log Forge

Discrete logarithms · generic algorithms · Pohlig–Hellman · index calculus

## What It Is

A browser-only laboratory that actually recovers discrete logarithms in finite fields, their prime-order subgroups, and a verified toy elliptic curve. It also shows how a validated static-DH oracle can surrender its long-lived exponent through Cheon’s attack. Every displayed exponent is checked with independent arithmetic before display. It is a teaching demo, not production cryptography.

Built to the [Crypto Lab master template](https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab/blob/main/audits/_MASTER-TEMPLATE.md). The original brief is included; scope corrections below are deliberate. Fleet chrome and accessibility machinery derive from MIT-licensed Crypto Lab work by Paul Clark.

## Exhibits

1. **Solver race:** brute force, BSGS, Pollard rho with Floyd, kangaroo, Pohlig–Hellman and index calculus. Actual generator orders and membership are checked first.
2. **Digit lifting:** prime-power digits, verified projections and CRT; a certified 128-bit smooth-order modulus; safe-prime and ZK Arena partial leaks.
3. **Tables and walks:** recorded baby/giant steps, rho exponent-pair collisions and measured tail/cycle lengths, and tame/wild kangaroo jumps. Step controls expose the actual records. Long traces are sampled.
4. **Index calculus:** smooth relations, full-rank linear algebra modulo q, Euler parity modulo 2, and CRT. Keep one precomputation and solve several targets. A fixed p=101 trace checks all four non-field division candidates.
5. **Weak group forge:** fresh targets with smooth order, short exponents, a small field, or a prime-order toy curve. Every solver gets the same calibrated budgets, and every outcome is shown.
6. **Cost and key lengths:** separate field/order axes, formula lines, discrete measured points, NIST's classical-strength table, and the historical Logjam results.
7. **Static DH oracle:** Cheon’s q−1 attack recovers a static Diffie–Hellman key from d validated oracle answers, then recomputes query-budget divisors for three real group orders.

## When to Use It

Teach why field size, order factorization, group representation and exponent range all matter. Prime order removes a smoothness advantage; it does not make a tiny field safe. Generic algorithms run unchanged over the curve and field group interfaces.

## Live Demo

[Log Forge](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-log-forge/). Pages publication follows unit, browser claims, accessibility and concrete mutation gates.

## What Can Go Wrong

- Generic BSGS/rho search the square root of the **order being searched**. The largest-prime-factor statement applies after Pohlig–Hellman decomposition; it is not a universal cost for an unsplit solver.
- A 128-bit modulus with smooth order can give up its exponent. The fixture carries a Lucas certificate using the complete factorization of p−1.
- Rho restarts on degenerate congruences. Non-invertible coefficients are gcd-reduced, and candidate exponents are checked.
- A partial CRT result is a congruence, not a full logarithm. Large digits are explicitly skipped.
- General index calculus is restricted to safe-prime fixtures below 2^64. Rank deficiency never yields an arbitrary answer. Subgroup logs lift through a full generator, then divide by the cofactor.
- A fair toy race can have several winners, including brute force on a tiny prime-order curve. The brief's exclusive-winner rule is replaced with disclosed equal budgets and actual outcomes; caps are not tuned to manufacture a result.
- Failed or capped attacks establish no security claim. Stopped runs do not report an invented memory count: it is marked “not captured.” Successful memory counts are group/table records, excluding traces and arithmetic temporaries.
- The static-DH exhibit implements only Cheon’s q−1 construction. It shows q+1 divisors but never attacks them. Its square-root speed-ups count search steps; each Cheon step is an exponentiation, so the group-operation saving is smaller.
- BigInt is variable-time. Browser measurements are not attack-cost forecasts. Input changes retire results; cancellation terminates a fresh worker. A bounded main-thread fallback is explicitly disclosed if workers cannot be created.

## Real-World Usage

Discrete-log assumptions support DH and many signatures/proofs. Classical generic attacks motivate large prime subgroup orders; finite-field index calculus requires much larger fields. A static key holder that returns raw v^α values adds a separate oracle-query attack surface. NFS is a formula here, not implemented. The 2015 Logjam measurements are attributed to the authors' infrastructure and vulnerable servers at that time.

Primary references: Katz–Lindell third edition Chapter 10; [HAC §3.6](https://cacr.uwaterloo.ca/hac/about/chap3.pdf); [Pollard 1978](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-1978-0491431-9); [Pohlig–Hellman 1978](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1978.1055817); [Shoup 1997](https://www.shoup.net/papers/dlbounds1.pdf); [Logjam](https://weakdh.org/imperfect-forward-secrecy-ccs15.pdf); [NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5 Table 2](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-57pt1r5.pdf); [Boneh–Shoup v0.6 §16.1.4 and Exercise 16.3](https://toc.cryptobook.us/); [Cheon, EUROCRYPT 2006](https://iacr.org/archive/eurocrypt2006/40040001/40040001.pdf); and [RFC 9497 §7.2.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9497#section-7.2.3). The NIST ECC ranges are preserved rather than presented as exact equalities.

## How to Run Locally

Node 22 or newer:

```sh
npm ci
npm run dev
```

## Related Demos

[Factor Forge](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-factor-forge/), [ZK Arena](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-zk-arena/), [ElGamal Plain](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-elgamal-plain/), [DH MITM](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-diffie-hellman-mitm/), [Function Key](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-function-key/), [Curve Lens](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-curve-lens/), [Hash Hunt](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-hash-hunt/).

The overlap review matches the sibling commits pinned in the brief. ZK Arena already implements partial Pohlig–Hellman; its parameters, not its attack code, are reused as a cross-implementation fixture. Existing BSGS attacks remain linked. Log Forge adds digit lifting, a generic cross-representation comparison and real index-calculus precomputation.

## Build & Verify

```sh
npm test
npm run build
npx playwright install chromium
npm run test:e2e
npm run test:mutations
```

32 local unit tests pass. They cover the three K–L worked examples, all four generic methods in both representations, membership, Hasse-certified curve order, the 128-bit Lucas certificate, PH's measured operation advantage on a prime-power subgroup, ZK Arena's 564522-modulus partial leak, rank deficiency, every collected relation, Euler parity, subgroup lifting, independent verifier isolation, worker decimal serialization, the static-DH fixture and oracle boundary, Cheon recovery for every offered d, and multiply-back/primality checks for every real-group factor. No coverage percentage is claimed.

Thirteen browser claims independently exponentiate displayed answers, check CRT residues, rederive index relations, verify the oracle chain and recovered key, recompute real-group factors/divisors, verify negative claims, inspect trace controls and assert stale-result retirement. Fourteen concrete mutations must build, move bundle bytes, fail a previously passing named claim, restore exactly and pass again. Accessibility drives the production build at 1280/320 pixels through success, refusal, intermediate trace and disclosure states using unchanged fleet contrast and non-text oracles.

Browser verification runs in CI when supported local browser control is unavailable. Pages and grouped Dependabot auto-merge are gated on the full suite. PR checks, manual dispatch, per-ref concurrency and post-merge deployment dispatch are included.

## Performance

Each original race calibrates primitive group-operation throughput in the executing browser, then applies the same 2,000–100,000-operation and 3-second caps to every method. The static-DH race measures Cheon first and applies one disclosed, larger cap to Cheon, generic BSGS, and rho. Exponentiation expands into counted operations; inversions count once and are separately reported. Oracle queries and server work are reported separately from attacker work. Index linear-algebra scalar operations are separate. A method can refuse a table or interval before allocating unbounded memory. Independent verification is outside attack counts.

Real-size groups appear only in formulas and the key-length table. The inspectable smooth-order and partial-leak fixtures demonstrate weaknesses; they are not production parameters. Elementary index-calculus asymptotics omit the unspecified constant and are not numerical predictions.

The Crypto Lab catalog integration records this lab’s concept, level, source evidence and fleet automation. Playwright port 4227 is unique across all 223 registered configurations; strictPort is enforced and existing servers are never reused.

oracle inputs still count as queries and validation checks, but do not charge a
membership exponentiation that was skipped. The page now distinguishes its fixed
raw-answer oracle from TLS: RFC 8446 §§7.1 and 7.4 feed the DH secret into HKDF;
key reuse alone does not expose this oracle. RFC 9497 §7.2.3 supplies the OPRF
connection. Mutation replay requires the owning assertion in a structured report;
crashes, skipped tests, and setup failures cannot count as kills.

Cancellation in degraded mode is checked before computation starts and on every
progress update or error, so a retired run cannot replace a newer result.

- A partial CRT result is a congruence, not a full logarithm. Large digits are explicitly skipped.
- General index calculus is restricted to safe-prime fixtures below 2^64. Rank deficiency never yields an arbitrary answer. Subgroup logs lift through a full generator, then divide by the cofactor.
- A fair toy race can have several winners, including brute force on a tiny prime-order curve. The brief's exclusive-winner rule is replaced with disclosed equal budgets and actual outcomes; caps are not tuned to manufacture a result.
- Failed or capped attacks establish no security claim. Stopped runs do not report an invented memory count: it is marked “not captured.” Successful memory counts are group/table records, excluding traces and arithmetic temporaries.
- The static-DH exhibit implements only Cheon’s q−1 construction. It shows q+1 divisors but never attacks them. Its square-root speed-ups count search steps; each Cheon step is an exponentiation, so the group-operation saving is smaller.
- BigInt is variable-time. Browser measurements are not attack-cost forecasts. Input changes retire results; cancellation terminates a fresh worker. A bounded main-thread fallback is explicitly disclosed if workers cannot be created.

readme:
# TESLA Broadcast

## What It Is

Implements an RFC 4082-style one-way HMAC-SHA-256 key chain, distinct MAC keys, an Ed25519-signed anchor, receiver safety check, and delayed-key broadcast authentication. Simulated sender and receiver clocks make the timing assumption inspectable. Not production crypto — a teaching demo. All material is generated in memory; this static site has no account, backend or key storage.

## Exhibits

1. Forge a shared-key MAC as one of its receivers.
2. Build a signed chain and verify a later disclosed key after dropped intermediate packets.
3. Set the true receiver clock lag and its assumed upper bound; spoof a packet after key disclosure and watch the real checks in order.
4. Calculate radio airtime and run 10,000 random truncated-tag guesses.
5. Read the sourced Galileo OSNMA adaptation note, with no OSNMA parsing or conformance claim.

## When to Use It

Use this to study the exact mechanism and its failure boundary. Do not use the toy implementation, keys or protocols in a deployed security system.

## Live Demo

[Open TESLA Broadcast](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-tesla-broadcast/) to drive the exhibits. The build uses Vite's `/crypto-lab-tesla-broadcast/` base for GitHub Pages.

## What Can Go Wrong

If the receiver assumes a lag smaller than its true lag, a packet forged after disclosure passes the safety test, key-chain verification and real MAC verification. The valid tag does not prove authorship to a third party after disclosure.

## Real-World Usage

Galileo OSNMA adapts TESLA, but this code does not implement its formats, authentication messages or receiver rules. Sender and receiver clocks and the network are simulated; signatures, MACs and hashes are real.

## How to Run Locally

```sh
npm ci
npm run dev
```

## Build & Verify

```sh

npm run build
npx playwright install chromium
npm run test:a11y
npm run test:mutations
```

readme:
# Next Number

## What It Is

Implements a four-digit toy LCG, Java SE 21 java.util.Random’s exact 48-bit recurrence, a 512-bit truncated LCG from Boneh–Shoup v0.6 §3.7.1, and an RFC 8439 ChaCha20 control. The 2-D lattice reduction and Java hidden-bit searches use exact BigInt arithmetic. Not production crypto — a teaching demo. All material is generated in memory; this static site has no account, backend or key storage.

## Exhibits

1. Guess the toy generator’s fourth output from its public recurrence.
2. Recover Java’s internal state from two consecutive nextInt values by checking all 2^16 hidden low bits; optionally search 2^22 low bits after a next(26) pair.
3. Recover a 512-bit LCG state from two truncated outputs with exact 2-D lattice reduction; measure 200 random multipliers.
4. Run the same next-bit predictor interface against toy, Java, lattice, and ChaCha20 and inspect the Wilson interval.
5. Observe simple frequency and run checks pass on a pinned Java seed even while the next outputs are predicted.

## When to Use It

Use this to study the exact mechanism and its failure boundary. Do not use the toy implementation, keys or protocols in a deployed security system.

## Live Demo

[Open Next Number](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-next-number/) to drive the exhibits. The build uses Vite's `/crypto-lab-next-number/` base for GitHub Pages.

## What Can Go Wrong

Java Random is not a cryptographic generator. Its output can look balanced while the published recurrence lets an adversary derive the next output. A measured half-win rate for this particular predictor against ChaCha20 is not a proof of security against all efficient predictors.

## Real-World Usage

Java documents Random as unsuitable for cryptographic use and recommends SecureRandom. Browser V8’s Math.random uses xorshift128+, not Java’s LCG; neither should supply unpredictable security tokens.

```sh
npm ci
```

readme:
# DVD Scramble

## What It Is

Implements the bit-serial, two-LFSR Content Scrambling System generator in Boneh–Shoup v0.6 §3.8. A 16-bit guess of one register algebraically determines the other 24-bit seed; the attack verifies known bytes and a separate 32-byte future. This is the book’s teaching variant, not a DVD player or the deployed CSS key hierarchy. Not production crypto — a teaching demo. All material is generated in memory; this static site has no account, backend or key storage.

## Exhibits

1. Clock the 17-bit and 25-bit registers and watch their bytes, carry and output.
2. Supply three to eight known bytes; a worker enumerates 65,536 smaller-register seeds and counts the actual survivors.
3. Independently verify the recovered key against 32 unseen output bytes.
4. Measure search throughput and extrapolate a 2^40 brute-force time, labelled as an extrapolation.

## When to Use It

Use this to study the exact mechanism and its failure boundary. Do not use the toy implementation, keys or protocols in a deployed security system.

## Live Demo

[Open DVD Scramble](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-dvd-scramble/) to drive the exhibits. The build uses Vite's `/crypto-lab-dvd-scramble/` base for GitHub Pages.

## What Can Go Wrong

Three known bytes leave 65,536 candidates. With more known bytes, the generator’s invertible adder lets a six-byte transcript often identify the entire 40-bit seed. The recovered-key verdict is an alarm, not a victory for the cipher.

## Real-World Usage

CSS was a historical DVD scrambling system. This repository does not use, parse, or decrypt DVD content. The book’s variant differs from deployed CSS in forced-bit placement and discarded early bytes.

## How to Run Locally

```sh
npm ci
npm run dev
```

## Related Demos

[LFSR Forge](https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-lfsr-forge) · [Export Grade](https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-export-grade) · [WEP Crack](https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-wep-crack)

## Build & Verify

```sh
npm test
npm run build
npx playwright install chromium
npm run test:a11y
npm run test:mutations
```

13 executed unit cases; 1,000 independently generated keys × 256 bytes checked across two implementations, plus key recovery under both byte conventions. The book variant has no published KAT, so the test routes are independent re-derivations. The replayable mutation harness contains 13 concrete source patches. Each run first passes its named baseline test, requires a non-empty diff, a successful build and changed JavaScript bundle hash, then requires the owning test to fail and restores the original hash. The Playwright suite contains nine claims tests plus two accessibility state drives at 1280px and 320px. It scans reachable desktop and mobile states for WCAG 2.1 A/AA issues and independently rederives displayed claims. GitHub Actions runs unit tests, production build and browser gate before deploying; it also gates Dependabot pull requests, groups minor/patch npm updates and dispatches a deploy after an automated merge.

## Performance

All runs are local to the browser. Work figures shown in the page are either actual counted operations or explicitly labelled mathematical estimates/extrapolations. Workers keep long searches cancellable where used. No speed number is a claim about a production deployment.

## Sources

- [Boneh–Shoup v0.6 §3.8](https://toc.cryptobook.us/)

---

*One of the browser demos in the [Crypto Lab](https://crypto-lab.systemslibrarian.dev/) suite.*

*"So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all for the glory of God." — 1 Corinthians 10:31*

## Deviations from the brief

- **Full carry is intentional (DV-BE1).** [Boneh–Shoup v0.6 §3.8](https://crypto.stanford.edu/~dabo/cryptobook/BonehShoup_0_6.pdf) prints an update based on x+y alone, omitting incoming carry. At x+y=255 with incoming carry=1, it contradicts the same section's mod-2^24 identity. This lab uses `sum=x+y+carry; z=sum&255; carry=sum>>>8`, consistent with the full addition in [libdvdcss css.c](https://people.freebsd.org/~wpaul/7_2_RELEASE/mplayer/css.c). No GPL source code was copied. A deterministic counterexample (s1=0x434c, s2=0x9cbcf2), plus 10,000 fresh random keys, checks the identity; a concrete book-rule mutation must fail.
- **Exhaustive counts are honest.** The displayed search actually enumerates all 65,536 guesses to count ambiguity. It cannot stop at the hidden true key without an oracle. The brief's “fewer than 65,536” fixture and average 2^15 conflate exhaustive enumeration with externally verified early stopping. The 200-random-key test retains and verifies the true key, records actual work of 65,536 per search, and separately measures its retrospective position. One measured run gave a mean position of 33,921.54; this is not a count claimed by the attack. Six public bytes usually identify one key, but can leave multiple candidates.
- **Private bytes verify, never select.** The original UI filtered all public candidates against 32 hidden bytes and could falsely announce recovery from only three public bytes. Recovery now requires exactly one candidate *before* private verification. Ambiguous sets stay undetermined. Typed public bytes have no private continuation and never receive a recovered-secret verdict.
- **Mutation runner hardening.** The old text-search runner could accept timeouts as kills. The structured-report runner rejects infrastructure failures, retries and wrong-test failures; checks actual build and bundle changes; and reruns the restored baseline. The obsolete no-worker-message mutation was replaced by an observation-loss mutation that fails an owning assertion instead of hanging.

## Audit verification

`src/css/audit.test.ts` checks the 10,000-key identity, 200 independently generated six-byte samples, ambiguity, impossible bytes, cancellation and worker boundaries. The 200-key test logs its measured mean and ambiguity count on each run (`npx vitest run src/css/audit.test.ts --reporter=verbose`). `e2e/reference.ts` independently implements the bit recurrence and enumerates survivors; browser tests recompute displayed keys, future bytes, counters, rate arithmetic and histogram counts. The full accessibility machinery is adapted from the Schnorr reference; no known non-text failures are exempted.

Counts: `npx vitest list --json` lists declarations; `npm test` expands parameter rows to 13 cases. `npx playwright test --list` lists 11 browser tests. `scripts/mutations.json` contains 13 entries. No tests are skipped.

Mutation restoration hashes the JavaScript files listed by each fresh Vite build manifest. Unreferenced files left by browser artifact collection are excluded; baseline, mutant and restored builds still have to satisfy every assertion and hash check.

readme:
# Twist Trap

## What It Is

Implements a 61-bit toy Montgomery ladder and affine short-Weierstrass arithmetic. Two static chosen-point services demonstrate five-query quadratic-twist and invalid-curve secret recovery; both input-validation toggles default ON. A separate verifier checks a recovered scalar against Bob’s public key. Not production crypto — a teaching demo. All material is generated in memory; this static site has no account, backend or key storage.

## Exhibits

1. Test a chosen x coordinate for curve or twist membership and run the same x-only ladder.
2. Switch off twist validation, query five exact-order twist points, solve small logs and CRT sign choices, and independently match Bob’s public x.
3. Switch off full-coordinate validation, send five points from alternate b′ curves and recover the full scalar.
4. Send an on-curve order-four point that passes the curve check, then remove the leak by clamping to a multiple of four.
5. Compute twist orders from published real-curve p and n values, and run RFC 7748 X25519 vectors through the lab’s own ladder.

## When to Use It

Use this to study the exact mechanism and its failure boundary. Do not use the toy implementation, keys or protocols in a deployed security system.

## Live Demo

[Open Twist Trap](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-twist-trap/) to drive the exhibits. The build uses Vite's `/crypto-lab-twist-trap/` base for GitHub Pages.

## What Can Go Wrong

An on-curve check does not remove a small subgroup on the curve; an all-zero output check does not prevent larger-order twist leakage on this toy fixture. Skipping full point validation permits scalar multiplication on other b′ curves regardless of the intended curve’s twist security.

## Real-World Usage

No real curve is attacked. The P-256, secp256k1 and Curve25519 table computes public group orders and divisibility; SafeCurves rho estimates are attributed estimates. Real attacks require a chosen-point service with a reused secret scalar.

name: AKE Ladder
subtitle: Authenticated key exchange · Boneh–Shoup ch. 21
description: Build authenticated key exchange and remove fields to see how replay, key exposure, and partner confusion arise.
why_it_matters: A shared key alone does not tell each party who holds it. Protocol fields bind the key to identities and a fresh session.
readme:
# AKE Ladder

## What It Is

Implements Boneh–Shoup v0.6 AKE1 over ristretto255, Ed25519, HKDF-SHA-256 and AES-GCM; each of six insecure variations has a scripted attack over real wire operations. Additional acts compute AKE2eg, AKE4eg and AKE5 key agreements and show forward-secrecy, identity-protection and honest-Q deniability intuitions. Not production crypto — a teaching demo. All material is generated in memory; this static site has no account, backend or key storage.

## Exhibits

1. Step the honest AKE1 certificate, signature, CCA encryption, identity check and channel binding.
2. Remove one of six protocol protections; compare both parties’ actual session-key fingerprints and partner identities, then restore the field and see the same attacker procedure rejected.
3. Record AKE1 and AKE2eg AES-GCM messages and leak a long-term key; contrast with a leak of ephemeral α.
4. Compare AKE2eg’s clear certificates with AKE4eg’s encrypted certificates; try a fake responder.
5. Check genuine and Q-fabricated AKE5 transcripts with the same group-key consistency equations.

## When to Use It

Use this to study the exact mechanism and its failure boundary. Do not use the toy implementation, keys or protocols in a deployed security system.

## Live Demo

[Open AKE Ladder](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-ake-ladder/) to drive the exhibits. The build uses Vite's `/crypto-lab-ake-ladder/` base for GitHub Pages.

## What Can Go Wrong

AKE1 authenticates its session but does not provide forward secrecy: a later leak of P’s decryption scalar reveals a recorded session key and the recorded application message. Omitting individual fields can instead expose the key, replay it, or cause identity misbinding.

## Real-World Usage

The CA and certificate encoding are a small teaching model. V6 uses an E_EG KEM with an AES-CTR DEM instead of the book’s trapdoor-function construction; the malleability is the taught point. AKE5’s demonstration is honest-Q intuition, not the formal simulator argument.

## How to Run Locally

```sh
npm ci
npm run dev
```

## Related Demos

[Protocol Checker](https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-protocol-checker) · [DH MITM](https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-diffie-hellman-mitm) · [TLS Handshake](https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-tls-handshake) · [Noise Pipe](https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-noise-pipe) · [Protocol Compose](https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-protocol-compose)

## Build & Verify

```sh
npm test
npm run build
npx playwright install chromium
npm run test:a11y
npm run test:mutations
```

73 executed unit cases cover the six live variations and their restored failures, honest binding, primitive known answers, and AKE2eg/AKE4eg/AKE5 exchanges. No published AKE1–AKE5 end-to-end test vectors exist. The replayable mutation harness contains 17 concrete source patches (13 verdict paths and the original four definition regressions). Each run first passes its named baseline test, requires a non-empty diff, a successful build and changed JavaScript bundle hash, then requires the owning test to fail and restores the original hash. The Playwright suite contains 15 claims tests and two accessibility state drives (1280px and 320px). It scans reachable desktop and mobile states for WCAG 2.1 A/AA issues and independently rederives displayed claims. GitHub Actions runs unit tests, production build and browser gate before deploying; it also gates Dependabot pull requests, groups minor/patch npm updates and dispatches a deploy after an automated merge.

## Performance

All runs are local to the browser. Work figures shown in the page are either actual counted operations or explicitly labelled mathematical estimates/extrapolations. Workers keep long searches cancellable where used. No speed number is a claim about a production deployment.

## Sources

- [Boneh–Shoup v0.6 chapter 21 and §12.4](https://toc.cryptobook.us/)
- [RFC 9496 ristretto255](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9496)
- [RFC 8032 Ed25519](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032)
- [RFC 5869 HKDF](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5869)

---

*One of the browser demos in the [Crypto Lab](https://crypto-lab.systemslibrarian.dev/) suite.*

*"So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all for the glory of God." — 1 Corinthians 10:31*

## Deviations from the brief

- The mutation runner uses structured Playwright reports, rejects timeouts, browser/setup failures and retries, requires the exact owning assertion, and reruns the restored test. Retaining the former text-search runner would incorrectly count infrastructure failures as kills. This intentional exception to the runner freeze matches Hash Hunt's hardened runner.
- The brief leaves its McGrew–Viega GCM case explicitly UNVERIFIED. The pinned multi-block substitute is NIST's [AES-GCM examples](https://csrc.nist.gov/CSRC/media/Projects/Cryptographic-Standards-and-Guidelines/documents/examples/AES_GCM.pdf), GCM-AES256 Example 2 (512-bit plaintext, no AAD, 128-bit tag). The actual AES-GCM wrapper is tested with the published IV through a test-only RNG mock.
- A finite set of leaked-signing-key decryption probes cannot prove forward secrecy. The page says exactly what was tried; DH security and erasure supply the cryptographic argument (Boneh–Shoup §21.3). The adversary receives the actual disclosed key and public recording. A negative-control unit test deliberately encrypts under that key and confirms the probe catches the exposure.

## Audit repair evidence

Protocol runs are coordinated in `src/ake/`; individual `src/attack/` modules receive public wire copies, corrupt-user signing capability or an explicitly leaked key. They cannot import honest state. Honest P creates the V1 application record; honest Q supplies V3's partner and binding. The ephemeral-alpha experiment replays a signed u to a fresh honest Q, derives the adversary's key, sends an application record, and checks Q's actual acceptance. The AKE4 forgery replays an authentic earlier signature on fresh DH values, with a successful verification of the original as its positive control.

Expandable educator inspectors include session keys and full bytes for verification; those inspector values are not inputs to the adversary. Browser tests independently encode tuples and use Node crypto for hashes, HKDF, AES-GCM and Ed25519; their AKE5 reference reimplements the equations over the public ristretto primitive. AKE1 post-leak decryption is independently recomputed from the disclosed scalar.

`src/kat/vectors.json` was extracted from primary texts, not recalled values: RFC 9496 A.1 (16) and A.2 (29); RFC 8032 §7.1 TEST 1, TEST 2, TEST 1024; RFC 5869 A.1/A.2; NIST SP 800-38A F.5.1's four blocks; NIST AES-GCM AES256 Example 2. The file records SHA-256 digests of the downloaded source files. URLs: [RFC 9496](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9496.txt), [RFC 8032](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032.txt), [RFC 5869](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5869.txt), [SP 800-38A](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-38a.pdf).

Counts: `npx vitest list --json` enumerates declarations in this Vitest version; `npm test` expands parameter rows to 73 cases. `npx playwright test --list` lists 17 browser tests. `scripts/mutations.json` has 17 entries. No tests are skipped.

readme:
# Clock Arithmetic

## What It Is

Exact, inspectable BigInt number theory underneath RSA and finite-field Diffie–Hellman: modular arithmetic, extended Euclid, Euler φ, multiplicative orders, generators, subgroups, generalized CRT and Montgomery reduction. The computations check their own preconditions and use independent routes where feasible. This is a small-number teaching lab, not production cryptography.

## Exhibits

1. **Wrap around:** reduce signed integers; draw discrete clocks through modulus 24 and residue strips above it; inspect addition and multiplication tables through 13.
2. **Undo multiplication:** step Euclid, check every Bézout row, derive a normalized inverse, and recognize shared-factor failures.
3. **Count units:** compare enumeration with the prime-factor formula. Unit lists paginate in groups of 200; the exact count includes all units.
4. **Watch powers cycle:** compare a walk with divisor-based order computation, check Euler/Fermat/Lagrange, and observe that Euler can hold for a cycle of length two.
5. **Generators and subgroups:** inspect every element’s order and every prime-factor generator check. A toy DH separates the possible-secret count from the number of guesses actually used.
6. **Recombine remainders:** step generalized CRT, reject incompatible congruences, deduplicate repeats, and use the lcm for compatible noncoprime moduli.
7. **Montgomery multiplication:** choose an explicit power-of-two radix, encode through REDC, inspect low-word cancellation, radix shifting and final subtraction, keep a product-and-square chain encoded, then decode once. A fixed 4,096-operation comparison measures setup, ordinary repeated work, Montgomery repeated work and final decoding separately.

## When to Use It

Use it to learn the arithmetic vocabulary before RSA, finite-field DH or discrete-log attacks. Predict each outcome before computing and compare the counterexamples. Do **not** use it to generate or protect real keys, test large numbers for primality, or benchmark real cryptographic attacks.

## Live Demo

[Open Clock Arithmetic](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-clock-arithmetic/). Predict first, then click Compute or an example to inspect every computed row. Each reveal answers its own fixed prediction using the arithmetic modules. Input changes cancel the Worker and retire dependent results; a no-op leaves them intact.

## What Can Go Wrong

An inverse requires gcd one. Euler requires a unit. A whole-group generator must pass the check for every prime dividing the group order. A proper prime-order subgroup is useful, while an order-two DH base is too small. Generalized CRT requires the gcd to divide each difference. The power-of-two Montgomery specialization requires odd N, R > N and the inverse-derived constant N′; the unreduced REDC candidate may still require one final subtraction. Correct mathematical refusals are informational; route disagreements and the deliberately tiny DH space are alarms.

The negative fixture uses a = 22 modulo 23: Euler, Fermat, divisibility of the order and return to one all pass, while only two shared secrets are possible. Passing a theorem’s precondition does not establish a useful cryptographic group size.

## Real-World Usage

RSA computes its private exponent using an inverse and often recombines CRT residues. [RFC 7919 Appendix A.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7919.html#appendix-A.1) specifies FFDHE’s g = 2 and prime subgroup order q = (p−1)/2. The p = 23 examples here are arithmetic models, not deployed parameters. [Montgomery’s original 1985 paper](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-1985-0777282-X) defines the residue representation and REDC method used in exhibit 7. Sunzi’s classical remainder problem supplies the CRT default; no historical date is asserted. Paar and Pelzl, *Understanding Cryptography* (2010), §§1.4, 6.3, 7.5.2 and 8.2 supply teaching context; no text or worked example is reproduced.

## How to Run Locally

```bash
npm ci
npm run dev
```

## Related Demos

- [Educational RSA](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-rsa-educational/) — the inverse becomes d; fast exponentiation traces.
- [RSA Forge](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-rsa-forge/) — Håstad’s attack and software-simulated CRT faults, both confirmed from executed source.
- [Prime Witness](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-prime-witness/) — Fermat as a primality test, and its liars.
- [Log Forge](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-log-forge/) — discrete-log algorithms and Pohlig–Hellman.
- [ElGamal Plain](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-elgamal-plain/) — full-group versus subgroup message encoding.
- [Residue Gate](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-residue-gate/) — squares and symbols.
- [DH MITM](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-diffie-hellman-mitm/) — the exchange and its authentication.
- [AES Anatomy](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-aes-anatomy/) — polynomial arithmetic over GF(2⁸).

## Build & Verify

```bash
npm ci
npm test
npm run build
npx playwright install chromium
npx playwright test --retries=0
node scripts/check-mutations.mjs
```

Fifty-nine unit cases include the original exhaustive arithmetic checks plus independent Montgomery REDC calculations, every valid T for N = 17, every input pair for every odd modulus through 99, explicit raw-candidate/final-subtraction traces, both sides of the 2³⁹ radix transition, the full 10¹² modulus boundary, invalid modulus/radix combinations, conversion through R², chained multiplication and identical fixed-work schedules. The original core ranges and pinned mathematical values are unchanged.

The 38 browser claims independently recompute reductions, multiplication-row permutations, Bézout identities, inverse ranges, unit counts, power walks, every prime-factor generator check, subgroup members, DH search space and guess position, CRT inverses/substitutions, and the Montgomery trace, chain and fixed-work result. The N = 9 fixture requires raw candidate 9 followed by subtraction to 0; the negative-input fixture requires canonical result 2 and every verdict to pass. Invalid even/unit/over-budget moduli, too-small radices and non-power-of-two radices have named informational refusals. The existing negative act-4 fixture and cancellation/input-budget gates remain intact.

Two accessibility tests scan every act and example at 1280px and 320px, including Montgomery’s valid traces and refusal states, arrival before computation, reveals and the composite counterexample. They retain axe, measured contrast, focus, hidden-state and overflow gates and the existing non-text baseline.

The mutation runner requires committed source and records 38 concrete mutations, including ten Montgomery cases and the existing two-patch cancellation mutation. Before building, it proves that every mutation owner selects exactly one browser test. Each case must pass that named baseline, produce a non-empty source diff, compile and move the bundle hash, fail by an assertion, then restore the exact bundle and pass again. It rejects missing/duplicate anchors, build failures, infrastructure errors, timeouts, empty/multiple selections, skips and retries as kills. Hosted CI preserves complete JSON and per-case logs after a successful gate, or whatever partial evidence was generated by an in-loop failure; failures before artifact creation remain visible in the workflow step log.


## Performance

Heavy computations and HTML preparation run in a cancellable Worker; the page reports their measured elapsed time. The Montgomery exhibit additionally separates context/encoding setup, an ordinary 4,096-operation loop, the matching encoded loop and final decoding. The encoded loop executes the implementation’s validation and trace-object work on every operation, so its single-run values are neither a general benchmark nor a constant-time claim. Factorisation is exact trial division through 10¹², counting through 10⁶, prime-group enumeration through 10⁴, and displayed wrap/walk experiments through modulus 10⁴. Inputs above the declared budget are refused. BigInt arithmetic stays exact above 2⁵³. Large unit lists are paginated, and wide data regions are keyboard-scrollable. Subgroup construction reuses one primitive root across every divisor instead of enumerating all generators again for each subgroup.

readme:
# AES Anatomy

## What It Is

A ten-act, inspectable implementation of AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256. Build finite-field arithmetic and the S-box, trace every round and inverse, then remove one layer and run an oracle-only attack beside the same attack on full AES. Real AES is the default; broken variants are opt-in teaching experiments.

## Exhibits

1. **Bytes are polynomials:** XOR, xtime, polynomial multiplication and extended Euclid; zero has no multiplicative inverse.
2. **Build the S-box:** derive all 256 entries and inverse entries; compute exhaustive DDT, LAT and affine-identity checks.
3. **Move and mix:** inspect both column matrices, all 69 square minors, structural byte dependencies and separately observed differences.
4. **Expand the key:** all 44/52/60 words, intermediate word operations, AES-256’s extra SubWord, and a one-bit key-change prediction.
5. **The whole cipher:** every round’s intermediate states, the omitted final MixColumns, and independent browser WebCrypto checks.
6. **Reverse the cipher:** step the inverse, then deliberately use forward keys or the wrong column matrix and observe the mismatch.
7. **Remove a layer:** affine inversion from one known pair, known-column transplantation, or a 256-query byte codebook. All four attacks show 32 fresh held-out successes and 32 failing control rows for full AES.
8. **Inject a fault, recover the key:** inject a declared one-byte fault before AES-128 round-9 MixColumns, compare correct/faulty ciphertexts, filter last-round-key quartets with inverse-S-box differentials, recover round key 10 from eight well-located faulty ciphertexts, reverse the key schedule, and verify the master key on a held-out plaintext. A recomputation example catches a one-sided fault but explicitly shows its common-mode limit; a wrong fault-location model fails without a recovery claim.
9. **Keep only accepted outputs, recover a byte:** clear a declared bit immediately after first-round SubBytes, continue the existing real AES-128 implementation, and classify the correct and fault-path ciphertexts by equality. A reproducible noisy experiment ranks all 256 first-key-byte guesses over increasing sample budgets, while an analytic population check and a secret-independent bit-flip control isolate the selection bias. Executable reject and infective cases show both when output selection is visible and how an exact clean-reference oracle recreates it.

## When to Use It

Use this lab to understand what each AES layer contributes and to distinguish invertibility, diffusion and avalanche from security. Use the traces to check your own learning implementation. Do not use this JavaScript implementation to protect real data: it is neither constant-time nor a hardened cryptographic library.

## Live Demo

[Open AES Anatomy](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-aes-anatomy/). Load the published FIPS keys or a reproducible seeded example. The shared state grid uses column-major indexing r + 4c. Changes retire derived state; cancelling or changing inputs terminates pending attack work.

## What Can Go Wrong

Wrong byte order, a missing AES-256 key-schedule operation, retaining MixColumns in the last round, using the wrong inverse, or assuming the wrong fault location can produce plausible-looking bytes. Independent published vectors and browser recomputation catch those errors. A singular linear map in an affine ablation is an implementation alarm, while failure to find a linear model for full AES is an expected control outcome.

The affine-only fixture has mean avalanche 61.5 bits, complete byte dependency computed from the keyed cipher’s 128 basis columns after two rounds, and a working keyed inverse. It is nevertheless broken by one known pair. Every displayed control row is computed and checked; a green-looking average is not a security argument. Partial byte codebooks retain unknown bytes as dots, and an absent splice column is refused.

## Real-World Usage

AES is specified by [FIPS 197-upd1 (2023)](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.197-upd1.pdf). In the absence of an application-profile standard specifying otherwise, [RFC 9846 §9.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846.html#section-9.1) requires a TLS-compliant application to support TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256; this is a support requirement, not a claim about measured HTTPS traffic. RFC 9846 obsoletes RFC 8446. Modes and authenticated encryption are separate from the block primitive taught here.

The DFA exercise follows the classic late-round AES fault equations described by Dusart, Letourneux & Vivolo, *Differential Fault Analysis on A.E.S.* (ePrint 2003/010): a one-byte fault before the penultimate-round MixColumns spreads to four bytes, and inverse-S-box relations constrain the last-round key. This browser model uses a known logical fault location and unknown nonzero fault value; it is not a physical fault-injection claim.

The accepted-output exercise distinguishes reliable ineffective fault analysis from statistical ineffective fault analysis. It clears one LSB-numbered bit of state byte 0 immediately after first-round SubBytes, continues real AES-128, and calls an execution unchanged only when the correct and fault-path ciphertexts are equal. The noisy model has a declared six-of-eight landing profile; misses and genuinely ineffective inductions are verifier-distinct but attacker-indistinguishable. Its finite-sample run draws plaintext bytes and landing events from the visible reproducible seed, while the separate 2,048-row census is labeled an analytic population check rather than sampled evidence. The ranker receives only selected plaintext bytes and the target bit, not the key, internal state, or per-attempt fault labels.

This mechanism follows [Clavier’s ineffective-fault analysis](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-74735-2_13) and Dobraunig et al., [*SIFA: Exploiting Ineffective Fault Inductions on Symmetric Cryptography*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/071). The protection boundary is informed by Daemen et al., [*Protecting against Statistical Ineffective Fault Attacks*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/536). Reject-on-detection visibly suppresses changed outputs. The bounded infective comparison returns a concretely transformed block on a detected mismatch: without a classifier, all attempts reach this selection-only ranker; with the correct clean ciphertext for the same plaintext, equality recovers the unchanged subset. That deterministic transform is not timing- or latency-oblivious, not a hardened countermeasure, and not an implementation of the 2020 paper’s circuit protections. The lesson recovers one AES-128 key byte in its declared model and makes no physical-injection, full multi-byte AES SIFA, timing, common-mode, or universal-defense claim.

Source data in `src/data/fips197.json` was transcribed from the standard’s S-box tables, all Appendix A expanded words, and Appendix B intermediate states. Appendix C vectors come from the superseded [FIPS 197 (2001)](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.197.pdf); the 2023 Appendix C instead points to online examples. No textbook figures, exercises or prose are reproduced.

## How to Run Locally

```bash
npm ci
npm run dev
```

- [AES Modes](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-aes-modes/) — build encryption schemes from a block cipher.
- [AEGIS Gate](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-aegis-gate/) — one genuine AES round inside another construction.
- [Glass Box](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-glass-box/) — white-box implementation attacks and key-schedule inversion.
- [Sleeve Check](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-sleeve-check/) — the S-box’s construction choices.
- [Biham Lens](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-biham-lens/) and [Matsui Line](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-matsui-line/) — how differential and linear biases support attacks.
- [Power Trace](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-power-trace/) and [Masked Core](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-masked-core/) — implementation leakage and countermeasures.

## Build & Verify

```bash
npm test
npm run build
npx playwright install chromium
npx playwright test --retries=0
node scripts/check-mutations.mjs
node scripts/measure-performance.mjs
```

Unit cases check all FIPS words and intermediate states, 400 seeded WebCrypto comparisons, 200 AES-192 round trips, exhaustive finite-field facts, all 69 minors, 200 seeded ablation-property cases, oracle import/arity and victim-key independence boundaries, held-out ordering/transcript separation, a memorising-attack canary, independently reconstructed invertible controls, singular and partial-codebook refusals, DFA recovery, and the IFA/SIFA mechanisms. Twenty browser claims independently recompute attack/control rows, fault witnesses and SIFA rankings, inspect all key words and both S-box tables (including fixed SHA-256 digests), verify every AddRoundKey XOR and field computation, and check verdict classes, score denominators, hidden panels and complete retirement. Two accessibility drives scan all ten acts and expanded results at desktop and 320px: axe A/AA and landmarks, measured visible/hidden text and nontext contrast, keyboard scrollers, focus and reflow. The nontext baseline is empty.

Forty-four scripted mutations cover the original cases, every test-honesty survivor, the DFA mechanism, and the SIFA ranker, real fault application, equality classifier, landing distribution, control, hidden-selection boundary and infection transform. Each must build into a different artifact, fail a named assertion with retries disabled, restore byte-for-byte, and pass its owning test again. `mutation-evidence.json` records executed results and named owning tests; [AUDIT_VERIFICATION.md](AUDIT_VERIFICATION.md) maps the added cases to their owners. The AES-256-only mutant also runs AES-128 controls to prove those paths still pass. GitHub Pages deployment depends on the complete unit/build/browser/mutation gate; grouped Dependabot changes use that same gate and explicitly dispatch deployment after merge.

## Performance

`performance-evidence.json` measures the same production modules compiled by Vite as a minified browser bundle. On Chromium 153, DDT/LAT/MDS/linear-order checks took at most 7.5 ms unthrottled and 36.9 ms with a 4× CPU slowdown. They remain on the main thread. Attack, verification and result preparation took up to 34.8 ms unthrottled and 180.5 ms under that slowdown, so the shared attack harness runs in a cancellable Worker. The slowdown is a simulation, not a physical-phone benchmark. Matrix rows are prepared once; wide matrices and traces are labelled keyboard-scrollable regions.

---

*One of the browser demos in the [Crypto Lab](https://crypto-lab.systemslibrarian.dev/) suite.*

*"So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all for the glory of God." — 1 Corinthians 10:31*

## Wide trails and reduced-round integrals

Act 3 checks ShiftRows column dispersion alongside all 69 MixColumns minors. It connects those hypotheses to the four-round, 25-active-S-box theorem, shows an observed trace separately, and makes the identity-permutation counterexample visible. Differential-trail probability and linear-trail correlation bounds are not differential/hull or full-cipher security bounds.

Act 10 runs a four-round AES-128 reduction: three ordinary rounds and a final round without MixColumns. An oracle-only attacker filters all 256 key-byte candidates using complete, disjoint Lambda-sets (up to six), reverses the round-4 schedule only when every byte is unique, and checks three separate held-out plaintexts afterward. It exposes ambiguous results rather than claiming unconditional recovery.

Source: Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen, *The Design of Rijndael: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)*, second edition, 2020. Theorem 9.5.1: printed pp. 140–143 / supplied PDF pp. 160–163. Integral attack: printed pp. 150–152 / supplied PDF pp. 170–172.

readme_sections.heading: What Can Go Wrong
readme_sections.text:
Wrong byte order, a missing AES-256 key-schedule operation, retaining MixColumns in the last round, using the wrong inverse, or assuming the wrong fault location can produce plausible-looking bytes. Independent published vectors and browser recomputation catch those errors. A singular linear map in an affine ablation is an implementation alarm, while failure to find a linear model for full AES is an expected control outcome.

The affine-only fixture has mean avalanche 61.5 bits, complete byte dependency computed from the keyed cipher’s 128 basis columns after two rounds, and a working keyed inverse. It is nevertheless broken by one known pair. Every displayed control row is computed and checked; a green-looking average is not a security argument. Partial byte codebooks retain unknown bytes as dots, and an absent splice column is refused.

card.title: Dedup Vault
card.copy: Compare fresh-key, local message-locked and server-aided encryption for equal files; measure deduplication and dictionary pressure, then separate possession, authorization, deletion, revocation and rotation.
card.review_note: Read the complete merged README, source, tests, learner interface and limits at this exact main commit. Two equal synthetic uploads execute fresh random AES-CTR keys, local first128(SHA-256(P || M)) message-locked derivation and RFC 9497 P256-SHA256 VOPRF derivation. Per-user RFC 5297 AES-SIV capsules bind scheme version, owner, reference and the complete data ciphertext; storage uses a digest only to select a bucket and deduplicates after full ciphertext-byte equality. The attack lesson computes local offline guesses, allowlisted per-principal/per-epoch online guesses, changed identities and epochs, proof tampering and key-server compromise. Separate executed cases distinguish bounded whole-ciphertext possession, reference authorization, last-reference deletion, prospective revocation with cached-copy limits and nonretroactive rotation. This is a DupLESS-shaped adaptation, not byte-for-byte DupLESS, a formal scalable proof-of-ownership protocol, process isolation, enforceable production rate limiting or a hardened storage service. Each derived AES-CTR key/counter pair is confined to one distinct plaintext value; repeats of that exact value intentionally reuse the pair and ciphertext. readme:
# Dedup Vault

## What It Is

Dedup Vault is an executable lesson about encrypted deduplication, message-locked encryption (MLE), and server-aided key derivation. Two synthetic users upload the same bytes in three modes, and the page computes which encrypted objects become equal, what storage is saved, and when a dictionary attacker can confirm a guess. The implementation uses real AES-128-CTR, AES-SIV-CMAC-256, SHA-256, and RFC 9497 P256-SHA256 VOPRF operations in the browser. Its storage, authentication, quota, and role boundaries are explicit teaching models, not hardened operational controls; this is not production storage software.

The page derives every displayed result from the TypeScript implementation in `src/`; it does not substitute hardcoded attack outcomes or storage totals.

### Fresh per-upload encryption

Each upload draws a new 128-bit data key and encrypts its file with AES-128-CTR. The counter is the all-zero 128-bit value, and each independently random key is used for one message. Equal plaintext uploads therefore normally have unequal data ciphertexts and occupy two content objects.

This is the no-deduplication comparison. It is not authenticated data encryption, and the demo does not recommend this construction as a production envelope format.

### Local message-locked encryption

The local mode follows the concrete convergent-encryption formula described in DupLESS, with one setup adaptation:

```text
data_key = first128(SHA-256(P || file))
Cdata    = AES-128-CTR(data_key, counter = 0, file)
```

DupLESS samples `P` as a random 128-bit public setup parameter. This lab instead fixes `P` to a reproducible, lesson-specific 16-byte application value in `src/crypto/aes.ts`. It separates this lesson's key space; it is not a password, salt, or defense against a dictionary attack. Equal files produce equal keys and equal `Cdata`, so a storage observer learns equality and an attacker can test low-entropy candidates offline.

### Server-aided derivation

The server-aided mode first computes a length-framed SHA-256 input over the scheme label, `P`, and the entire file. It then runs RFC 9497 VOPRF mode with the P256-SHA256 suite:

```text
input    = SHA-256(frame("dedup-vault/v1/voprf-input", P, file))
output   = VOPRF.Finalize(input, blind, evaluated, blinded, public_key, proof)
data_key = first128(output)
Cdata    = AES-128-CTR(data_key, counter = 0, file)
```

The client pins a public key before its request sequence and verifies the DLEQ proof against that key during `Finalize`; a changed proof, evaluated element, or coherent response under a substitute key is rejected. The proof establishes consistency with the pinned key, not that the key is authentic. Authentic public-key provisioning is outside the model. The modeled key server accepts only an allowlisted principal label before evaluation and allows exactly `q` successful requests per principal and epoch. That label represents the result of an external authentication step; this lab does not implement an authentication protocol.

This is a modern P-256 VOPRF adaptation of the server-aided idea in DupLESS. DupLESS used a blind-RSA OPRF, so its original proof does not automatically establish this substituted construction. The model demonstrates the boundary: rate limiting can delay a dictionary search, but additional identities, later epochs, collusion, or key-server compromise expand or remove that online boundary.

### Per-user key capsules

Each user has a distinct wrapping key, and each reference has a distinct capsule. The 16-byte data key is wrapped with RFC 5297 AES-SIV-CMAC-256 under a 32-byte combined key containing two AES-128 subkeys. This is another explicit adaptation: DupLESS section 6 uses an HMAC-SHA256/AES-CTR SIV construction, produces a 384-bit `Ckey`, and includes path/name handling that this lesson omits. Four associated-data components here bind the capsule to:

1. the capsule scheme and version;
2. the owner identity;
3. the reference identifier; and
4. the complete data ciphertext.

Changing any bound value, the capsule, or the wrapping key makes opening fail. Owner and reference strings must be well-formed Unicode so UTF-8 encoding cannot merge distinct JavaScript strings through replacement-character substitution. The storage layer deduplicates `Cdata` only after complete byte equality; its SHA-256 index only selects a candidate bucket. A test injects an index collision and proves unequal ciphertexts remain separate.

The displayed “stored bytes” deliberately counts unique data-ciphertext bytes plus capsule bytes. It excludes object indexes, owner/reference strings, maps, allocator overhead, and protocol traffic. Both logical data bytes and the narrower physical-data ratio remain visible so capsule overhead is not silently presented as saved data.

## Exhibits

1. **Equal file, three encryption choices** compares actual keys, ciphertext equality, object counts, capsules, bytes, and the data-deduplication ratio.
2. **Dictionary pressure and the online boundary** computes a local offline hit and miss, server-aided guesses inside and beyond `q`, a principal absent from the allowlist, separate principal budgets, a later rate epoch, key-server compromise, and proof tampering.
3. **Who learns what?** separates client, key-server, storage-server, storage-only-attacker, allowlisted guessing-client, and combined key-server-plus-ciphertext-compromise views.
4. **Boundaries: possession, authorization, deletion, revocation, rotation** executes possession, authorization, replay, reference-count deletion, prospective revocation, and key rotation.
5. **Construction, adaptation, and limits** keeps the adaptation, primitive choices, primary sources, and nonclaims visible.

The possession exercise uses a fresh nonce and a short hash response over that nonce and the complete modeled ciphertext. It saves retransmitting the object, but both sides read the whole object. It shows why a blob identifier alone is not possession and why possession is not authorization; it is not the formal, leakage-resilient, scalable proof-of-ownership construction of Halevi, Harnik, Pinkas, and Shulman-Peleg.

## When to Use It

- Use it to compare randomized and deterministic encrypted storage, because the same input is executed through all three modes with measured equality and byte accounting.
- Use it to study offline versus rate-limited dictionary attacks, because candidate ciphertexts and VOPRF queries are computed rather than narrated.
- Use it for reviewing deduplication boundaries, because possession, authorization, deletion, revocation, rotation, and compromise are separate executable cases.
- Do not use it to protect real files or operate a key service, because it is a demo app and does not provide hardened operational controls.

## Live Demo

Open [Dedup Vault on GitHub Pages](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-dedup-vault/). Change the synthetic file, run all experiments, compare physical storage across modes, inspect each role's view, and follow the computed attack and lifecycle outcomes.

## What Can Go Wrong

- All roles execute in one browser origin. The UI does not establish process, network, hardware, or secret isolation.
- Deterministic data ciphertext leaks file equality, length, upload timing, and reference/deletion patterns to storage.
- Low-entropy files remain guessable. A per-principal request budget delays guesses; it does not create entropy or solve Sybil, distributed, eventual, or compromise attacks.
- The deterministic modes deliberately repeat an AES-CTR key and counter when the exact same plaintext value is repeated, exposing the equality needed for deduplication and departing from ordinary CTR counter uniqueness. The model intends each derived key for only one distinct plaintext value; using that key/counter pair for any different plaintext exposes the plaintext XOR.
- The data ciphertext has no independent authentication tag. The authenticated per-user capsule commits to the complete ciphertext, so an authorized client detects changes when opening the capsule; this is not a general multi-writer storage design.
- The capsule detects unauthenticated byte changes, but without trusted external version state it does not detect rollback or replay of an older valid `(Cdata, capsule)` pair.
- Revocation blocks future modeled storage reads and VOPRF derivations. It cannot erase plaintext, ciphertext, or keys already cached by a formerly authorized client.
- Rotation changes future VOPRF output and ciphertext. It neither rewrites nor revokes old objects.
- JavaScript execution is not guaranteed constant-time.
- [Noble Curves' security record](https://github.com/paulmillr/noble-curves/blob/main/README.md#security) identifies an all-scope Trail of Bits review of version 2.3.0; this lesson pins the later [2.4.0 release](https://github.com/paulmillr/noble-curves/releases/tag/2.4.0). [Noble Ciphers' security record](https://github.com/paulmillr/noble-ciphers/blob/main/README.md#security) identifies an all-scope Cure53 review of version 1.0.0, while [AES-SIV was introduced in version 2.1.1](https://github.com/paulmillr/noble-ciphers/releases/tag/2.1.1). Upstream vector and self-audit evidence is useful, but this exact AES-SIV code is not covered by that independent audit.

See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) and [docs/a-d-01-brief.md](docs/a-d-01-brief.md) for the threat model and acceptance mapping.

## Real-World Usage

Encrypted backup and object-storage designs may seek deduplication so repeated content consumes one physical object. Message-locked encryption makes that possible by deriving stable encryption material from the message, but the equality signal and low-entropy dictionary risk are part of the construction, not incidental implementation bugs. DupLESS introduced a server-aided approach that makes each guess interact with a rate-limited key server; this lab preserves that teaching boundary while clearly labeling its modern P-256 VOPRF and RFC 5297 capsule substitutions.

Primary sources:

- Mihir Bellare, Sriram Keelveedhi, and Thomas Ristenpart, [Message-Locked Encryption and Secure Deduplication](https://eprint.iacr.org/2012/631), EUROCRYPT 2013.
- Mihir Bellare et al., [DupLESS: Server-Aided Encryption for Deduplicated Storage](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity13/technical-sessions/presentation/bellare), USENIX Security 2013.
- [RFC 9497: Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9497).
- [RFC 5297: Synthetic Initialization Vector (SIV) Authenticated Encryption](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5297).
- [NIST SP 800-38A: Block Cipher Modes of Operation](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/38/a/final).
- Shai Halevi et al., [Proofs of Ownership in Remote Storage Systems](https://eprint.iacr.org/2011/207).

## How to Run Locally

Use Node.js 22.13 or newer within the 22.x line, Node.js 24.x, or Node.js 26 or newer. That range is the intersection supported by the locked development toolchain; the runtime Noble dependencies themselves require Node 20.19 or newer.

```sh
npm ci
npm run dev
```

The application is a static browser lesson with no backend, accounts, or persistent secrets.

## Related Demos

- [Envelope KMS](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-envelope-kms/) compares randomized envelope encryption, wrapping, rewrapping, and compromise scope.
- [OPAQUE Gate](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-opaque-gate/) gives an OPRF a different role inside a password-authentication protocol.
- [ORAM Vault](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-oram-vault/) examines access-pattern leakage that ciphertext confidentiality alone does not hide.

## Build & Verify

The unit suite contains 38 tests. It anchors RFC 9497 Appendix A.3.2.1 P256-SHA256 VOPRF key derivation/proof/output, RFC 5297 Appendix A.1 deterministic and Appendix A.2 nonce-based AES-SIV, and NIST SP 800-38A Appendix F.5 AES-128-CTR. Negative tests cover proof, evaluated-element, public-key, associated-data, ciphertext, capsule, and key tampering; quota and allowlist boundaries; retrieval and collision handling; deletion, replay, authorization, revocation, rotation, and dictionary cases.

The browser suite contains 18 learner-claim and accessibility/reflow tests. Claim tests independently recalculate visible byte counts and decrypt displayed AES-CTR ciphertext with WebCrypto. Accessibility tests cover axe violations and incomplete results, arithmetic text and non-text contrast, generated content, keyboard navigation, fleet chrome, the dark-only theme under both operating-system color preferences, reduced motion, and 320/380/390/768/1440-pixel reflow. The mutation runner starts from a clean committed baseline and requires all 24 concrete source mutations to move the built bundle and fail their named owning test.

```sh
npm run format:check
npm run typecheck
npm run lint
npm run test:coverage
npm run build
npm audit --audit-level=high
npx playwright install chromium
npm run test:claims
npm run test:a11y
npm run test:mutations
```

`npm run ci` runs the static, unit, coverage, and build portion. GitHub Actions runs the complete gate before publishing GitHub Pages. The deployed lesson includes the runtime dependency copyright and MIT license text at [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-dedup-vault/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt).

The lab is MIT licensed; see [LICENSE](LICENSE) and [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

name: DC-net
